name: Availability Heuristic
description: People judge what is likely, frequent, or important by how easily examples come to mind. Vivid, recent, or memorable cases therefore feel more common than they really are.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to risk messaging, incident dashboards, search/recommendation surfaces, newsfeeds, and research synthesis: what the interface makes easiest to recall or imagine can distort later judgments.
prevalence_note: A core Kahneman/Tversky bias taught in essentially every behavioral-science-for-design or decision-bias curriculum, especially for risk communication and research interpretation.

findings.description: People judge the frequency or probability of an event by the ease with which instances or scenarios of it come to mind (availability), rather than by actual frequency — demonstrated experimentally (e.g. participants judging that more English words begin with the letter K than have K as the third letter, when the reverse is true, because words are more easily retrieved by first letter). Availability is driven by factors unrelated to true frequency, such as recency, salience, and imaginability, producing systematic and predictable judgment errors.
findings.source_title: Availability: A Heuristic for Judging Frequency and Probability

applications.title: Media coverage made pandemic crime feel like it was rising while it was actually falling
applications.description: During the COVID-19 pandemic, constant media coverage of isolated incidents and warnings about potential lockdown-related crime created a widespread public perception that crime was increasing. A research review criticized outlets including The Washington Post and CNN for surface-level analysis and reliance on anecdotal reports. In fact, most crime types declined sharply during this period: Pittsburgh, New York City, San Francisco, Philadelphia, Washington D.C., and Chicago all saw overall crime drop by at least 35%, with drug crime down more than 65% in many cities.
applications.industry_context: news media / public perception of crime
applications.ethical_note: This documents a real gap between media-driven public perception and actual crime statistics, not a persuasion or product-design case -- there is no single actor deliberately manipulating perception for gain here, just an emergent effect of how vivid, repeated coverage of isolated incidents shapes availability-based judgment at a societal scale.
